v4 findings: how the underwater voice link behaves, and why

November 11–12, 2026. This report explains what the v4 simulation campaign shows about LED colors, photodiodes, water types, lenses, ambient light and circuit settings, and gives the reason behind each result. Everything is calculation and simulation; nothing was measured on the team's hardware. Clayton's receiver, P6 and the v2 and v3 proposals are unchanged. Where a receiver "preset" is named, it is one of these:

PresetWhat it is
Oct 28 receiverClayton's October 28 schematic with the six fixes from v1: MTD5052W photodiode into the LMH34400 amplifier
v2S1337-1010BR photodiode, FBH450-40 blue filter, OPA2314 amplifier with 22 kΩ feedback
v2 + hoodv2 with the tube hood. This is the December demo build
v3v2 + hood with a 100 kΩ amplifier, the ambient-light servo and unity-gain filters

Terms used throughout:

TermMeaning here
P6the transmitter board, revision B2.1-HW-P6, as built
P1, R41on P6: the microphone preamp's gain trimmer (29.7 kΩ as built), and the resistor that senses and so sets the LED current (2 Ω as built: 188 mA average)
limiter, compressorP6's limiter clamps the LED current between 75 and 300 mA so loud speech cannot switch the LED off or overdrive it. A compressor (the SSM2167 option of v3) turns its gain down for loud speech and up for quiet speech
front end, overloadthe photodiode and the first amplifier. It overloads when the steady photocurrent drives that amplifier to its supply rail; the output is then useless and the row is flagged, not counted
servoin v3, a slow loop that removes the steady (ambient) part of the photocurrent so the first amplifier does not overload
hiss, humhiss is random noise (from the receiver, from the transmitter, and shot noise). Hum is the 120 Hz flicker of mains lamps and its harmonics
STOIan intelligibility score from 0 to 1 computed from the output audio (section 8)
dB of light, dB of SNR1 dB more light on the photodiode is 2 dB more SNR while the noise stays fixed, because SNR is a ratio of electrical powers and the photocurrent is proportional to the light
matched filterthe optical band-pass filter chosen for an LED's color (not the communications term)
condensera short-focus lens in front of the photodiode that gathers light over its whole aperture onto the detector
flat port, domethe window in front of the LED or photodiode: a flat plate, or a hemisphere centred on it
Beer–Lambertthe rule that light falls by a fixed fraction per metre of water. Used with the total attenuation it counts every scattered photon as lost
Jerlov types, Petzold, NTUJerlov's classes of ocean water, from clearest (I) to coastal (1C–9C); Petzold's three measured waters; and the turbidity unit that pool codes use
engines A, B, Cthree ways of solving the same link model: the full ngspice waveform simulation (A), a fast waveform version (B) and a formula version (C); see the README

Unless a section says otherwise, the conditions are P6 as built with its royal-blue LED, 15 ft of clear pool water, both ends aligned, indoor light (0.5 W/m² on the receiver with a flat spectrum, 5 % smooth flicker), normal speech (89 dB SPL at the microphone) and the receiver volume at maximum. SNR means the 300–3000 Hz signal-to-noise ratio at the headphones; the team's charter target is 14 dB, called the requirement below.

What the campaign found

  1. Four different things can limit the link, and which one is in charge decides what helps. They are the transmitter's own noise, the receiver's own noise, shot noise from light, and lamp hum. A change that is worth 20 dB against one of them is worth nothing against another (section 1).
  2. The photodiode was most of the original problem. Putting the S1337 into Clayton's circuit, with nothing else changed, moves the result at 15 ft from −42.7 dB to +14.1 dB. The new amplifier adds 16 dB, the filter and hood 3 dB, and the v3 front end 8 dB (section 2).
  3. Royal blue is the right LED for a large silicon photodiode in clear water; green is only better for the MTD5052W. A green XP-E2 gives 6.5 dB less than royal blue into the S1337, because it makes less than half the light per ampere. Into the MTD5052W it gives 10.5 dB more, because that photodiode is built for green (section 3).
  4. A lens on the LED is the largest single gain available, and it is cheap. A 34° lens (Carclo 10196, a few dollars) adds 17 dB at 30 ft, still works 20° off axis, and carries as far as eight bare LEDs. At 15 ft even that widest lens puts v3 within 1 dB of a ceiling near 51.7 dB that the transmitter's own noise sets, so narrower lenses buy range, not quality (section 6).
  5. Lamp flicker with harmonics is still the main risk, and what helps against it is narrowing what the receiver looks at. A bigger photodiode does nothing. A lens on the LED (+18 to +31 dB), a longer hood (+12 dB) and a narrower filter (+7 dB) help. Under hum a 1.2 mm² photodiode behind a condenser lens beats the 100 mm² S1337 behind its hood by 36 dB, but only within about 3° of the transmitter's direction (section 7).
  6. By the intelligibility score, hum hurts speech less than hiss does. The 14 dB requirement corresponds to an intelligibility score (STOI) of 0.75. Hiss-limited speech needs 13.5 dB to reach it; hum-limited speech reaches it at about 4 dB. v3's flicker case fails on SNR (10.9 dB) and still scores 0.81. This needs a listening check (section 8).
  7. Above about 25 dB, more SNR buys nothing a listener can use. v3's advantage over the December build is range (51 ft against 36 ft to 14 dB) and margin, not quality at 15 ft (section 8).
  8. Beer–Lambert is far too pessimistic in cloudy water for this kind of link. A photon-tracing study shows that most of the light scattered out of a bare LED's beam still reaches the receiver: about 94 % for a wide receiver and 82 % for a hooded one. With that included, a pool at the legal turbidity limit costs the December build about 9 ft of range instead of 21 ft (section 5).
  9. The MTD5052W can be made to pass at 15 ft, but only with a lens in front of it. With a 10 MΩ amplifier, a green LED and a condenser lens it reaches 48 dB on axis, with a field of view of about ±3° (section 4).
  10. On the transmitter, the cheapest gains are the preamp trim and a second LED. Below the ceiling, P1 at 60 kΩ is worth 5.4 dB, a second LED 6 dB, the compressor 9 dB. Doubling the LED current is worth only 4.3 dB. By the intelligibility score, 60 kΩ already costs a loud talker and more than 60 kΩ costs a normal one, because the limiter clips them. A quiet and a very loud talker differ by 22.5 dB (section 9).
  11. The receiver's volume control is in the wrong place for long range. It sits before the last gain stage, so a volume set at 3 ft and carried to 30 ft costs v3 up to 26 dB. After the first amplifier, no other receiver component value moves the SNR by more than about 2 dB. The first amplifier's feedback resistor is the one that matters: 100 kΩ in place of 22 kΩ in the December build is worth 9 dB indoors, slightly more than v3's 8 dB advantage at 15 ft (sections 4 and 9).
  12. If the pool lights do not flicker with harmonics, the December build passes at 15 ft in every one of the 1,188 random draws of what is not yet known that have smooth flicker. In the 812 draws with rectified flicker, 22 % pass. With a 34° lens on the LED, 86 % of all 2,000 draws pass, and of the 400 draws that were also scored for intelligibility, 96 % reach the score that goes with 14 dB (section 10).
  13. The fast engines agree with the full ngspice waveform simulation within 0.3 dB (nine runs in ten within 0.15 dB), which is what allowed about 833,000 configurations to be simulated in one night (section 11).

The data behind every statement is in data/ and tables/; the page explorer/vlc_v4_explorer.html lets you change one part at a time and watch the result.

1. The four limits

The receiver hears the speech plus four kinds of unwanted signal. The figure shows, for three receivers, what the SNR would be if only one of them existed. The black curve is the real result: it follows whichever colored curve is lowest.

LimitWhere it comes fromHow it changes with the linkWhat helps
Transmitter noiseP6's microphone preamp. It is transmitted along with the speech.It scales with the speech, so the ratio is fixed at about 51.7 dB whatever the optics.A quieter preamp, a louder microphone signal. Optics do nothing.
Receiver noiseThe amplifier and its resistors. A fixed amount.Fixed, so SNR follows the signal power: every 1 dB of light is 2 dB of SNR. Doubling the distance costs 12 dB plus the water.Anything that puts more signal current into the amplifier: detector area, lenses, a better-matched color. And a quieter amplifier.
Shot noiseLight arrives as separate photons, so any steady photocurrent (mostly ambient light) carries noise that grows as its square root.Ambient current grows with detector area, so area helps only 1 dB per dB here.Less ambient on the detector (filter, hood), more signal.
Lamp humMains-powered lamps flicker at 120 Hz. If the flicker has harmonics, they fall inside the speech band.Hum and signal both grow with detector area, so area cancels out completely.Less ambient per unit of signal: lens on the LED, hood, narrower filter.

At 15 ft the presets sit like this (SNR if only that noise were present, dB):

PresetAll noiseShot onlyReceiver onlyTransmitter onlyHum only (smooth flicker)
Oct 28 receiver−42.71.1−42.751.438.5
v232.442.332.951.799
v2 + hood32.748.332.951.7114
v340.948.242.351.7114

Three things follow from this table.

  • Every preset is limited by its own amplifier at 15 ft in indoor light. That is why v3's quieter amplifier is worth 8 dB, and why the hood, which only removes ambient light, is worth 0.3 dB here.
  • The Oct 28 receiver is 44 dB below what its own photodiode's shot noise would allow. Its amplifier (an LMH34400, built for lidar pulses) has about 21 pA/√Hz of noise in the speech band; v2's has 2.05 and v3's 0.66.
  • Nothing can exceed about 51.7 dB. Inside about 5 ft, or with a lens on the LED, the v2 and v3 designs come within 1 to 2 dB of that ceiling and stay there.

The same thing by frequency, from the ngspice analyses of each receiver at its 15 ft operating point (tables/receiver_response.md):

  • What they pass. v2 and v3 have the same band. Their fifth-order high-pass is 52 dB down at 120 Hz and 22 dB down at 240 Hz, but only 5.6 dB down at 360 Hz and 0.4 dB at 480 Hz. Flicker that is a pure 120 Hz tone is removed; the harmonics of rectified flicker from 360 Hz up are not, which is where section 7 starts. The Oct 28 receiver is only 17 dB down at 120 Hz.
  • Their own noise. At the preset volume the Oct 28 receiver has 38 pA/√Hz at 300 Hz falling to 12 at 3 kHz; v2 + hood has 8 at 300 Hz and about 2 from 1 to 3 kHz; v3 has 2.7 at 300 Hz and 0.7 to 0.9 from 1 to 3 kHz. The shot noise of the steady photocurrent in indoor light is 0.37 pA/√Hz behind the filter and hood. That is below every receiver's own noise, which is the first point above in other words.

The receiver volume matters in one specific way. The volume control sits before a fixed ×310 gain stage, so turning it down lowers the speech but not that stage's own hiss. At 15 ft, v3 gives 40.9 dB at full volume, 40.4 dB at −6 dB, 34.3 dB at −20 dB and about 1 dB at −55 dB. The grids in this report use full volume, which is the link's best case; a listener who turns the volume far down at long range would hear more hiss than these numbers say.

The first step deserves a caution. The model's LMH34400 noise does not depend on the photodiode's capacitance, and the S1337 has 1100 pF. The real result of that swap would probably be lower than 14 dB.

Keeping the MTD5052W instead, the same kind of ladder reads: OPA2314 at 22 kΩ, −23.4 dB; at 100 kΩ, −13.9 dB; at 10 MΩ, +0.9 dB (10.7 dB in the dark); with a green LED as well, 11.4 dB (20.8 dB in the dark); and with a condenser lens in front of it, 47.8 dB. Section 4 explains each of those.

Why royal blue wins with a silicon photodiode.

  • Light per ampere. Blue InGaN LEDs are the most efficient LEDs made. At the same current a green XP-E2 emits less than half the optical power (the "green gap"), and amber a quarter. This is the largest term for every color from cyan to amber.
  • Water. Clear water absorbs least between about 420 and 480 nm. Over 15 ft, green loses 1.3 dB more than blue and red loses 10–14 dB more.
  • Detector response. Silicon responds better toward the red (0.25 A/W at 450 nm, 0.32 at 525 nm, 0.42 at 660 nm), but that recovers only 2–4 dB.
  • Beam. LEDs with a narrower viewing angle put more of their light on the axis. The 80° OSLON green gains 7 dB that way and nearly matches royal blue; it is a lens effect, not a color effect, and section 6 covers it.

Why the MTD5052W is different. Its response is a narrow peak at 520 nm: 0.30 A/W there, and 0.027 A/W averaged over the royal-blue LED's spectrum (0.021 at 450 nm). Moving to green gains it 19 dB of response, which more than pays for green's 7 dB of lost light. It is also steep at the blue end, about 6 % per nanometre at 450 nm. If the LED's wavelength is shifted by ±8 nm (the P6 order code allows a 10 nm spread), its result moves from −17.6 to −10.1 dB, while the S1337's moves 0.5 dB (tables in c_led_bins). So any measurement with the MTD5052W and a blue LED depends on which LED bin was delivered.

Higher-output blue LEDs are worth about 1.4 dB. The XP-G3, XT-E and OSLON deep blue each gain that much over the XP-E2 on P6. For the first two about half comes from more light per ampere and half from a slightly narrower beam; the OSLON's gain is all beam.

Cool white works as well as royal blue into an unfiltered S1337, because it is a blue LED with a phosphor and the photodiode collects the phosphor light too. Behind the 450 nm filter it loses 11 dB.

With the matched filter and the hood the order is the same, except that blue 465 edges ahead of royal blue under white-LED lamps ("matched" here means the optical band-pass filter chosen for that LED's color). In bright white-LED light (5 W/m²) at 15 ft: royal blue with FBH450-40, 36 dB; blue 465 with FBH470-40, 36 dB; cyan with FBH500-40, 30 dB; green with FBH520-40, 27 dB; photo red with FBH650-40, 26 dB (tables/filters_by_led_bright.md).

4. Photodiodes and the amplifier behind them

Forty-four photodiode entries were modelled, about forty distinct parts from 1.1 to 613 mm² (the MTD5052W appears with three readings of its capacitance).

Area is worth 2 dB per dB when the amplifier is the limit and 1 dB per dB when light is. In the dark (blue points) the SNR climbs 20 dB for every tenfold increase in area, because a larger detector collects more signal and the amplifier noise stays put. In room light without a filter (orange points) the climb flattens toward 10 dB per tenfold as the detector grows, because the larger detector collects more ambient light too and its shot noise takes over from the amplifier. Against lamp hum it would not climb at all (section 7).

Capacitance is the price of area, and some large photodiodes are not worth it. A photodiode's capacitance multiplies the amplifier's voltage noise. The S1337-1010BR has 1100 pF for 100 mm². The S2387-1010R and S12915-1010R have the same area with 12,000–13,000 pF, and in the dark reach 38–39 ft where the S1337 reaches 53 ft. The 613 mm² PIN-25DP has 60,000 pF and a weaker blue response, and ends up below the 100 mm² S1337 in the dark.

Range to 14 dB for a bare detector on the v3 amplifier (royal blue, clear pool; tables/pd_range.md has all 44):

A 33 mm² photodiode still has 18 dB of margin at 15 ft, and one of 8 mm² has 9 dB. Below about 6 mm² only a few dB of margin are left at 15 ft. These are the best parts of each size: blue response differs by up to 15 dB between photodiodes of the same area, and four of the seven parts of 7 to 8 mm² in the table file are at or below 14 dB.

The MTD5052W. Three things hold it back, in this order.

  1. Its response to the royal-blue LED, 0.027 A/W against the S1337's 0.25: 19.4 dB of signal.
  2. Its area, 1.3 mm² against 100: 37.5 dB of signal.
  3. Its capacitance, probably. Marktech's 2021 datasheet gives 500–700 pF at 5 V reverse bias, which v1–v3 did not know (they assumed 5 pF). On a 100 kΩ amplifier that makes no difference (−13.9 dB against −14.0 dB), because the feedback resistor's own noise dominates. On the 10 MΩ amplifier that the MTD5052W needs (with the green LED and the lens below), it costs 0.6 dB at 15 ft and 2.2 dB at 30 ft. The Oct 28 circuit's LMH34400 is designed for a few picofarads at its input; its noise with 600 pF is not modelled here and is probably worse than simulated.

What gets it to 14 dB at 15 ft, from the waterfall batch (indoor light):

The condenser lens is what does it: a 23 mm aperture focused onto a 1.3 mm² detector collects about 130 times the light. The cost is the field of view. The signal falls from 2° off the receiver's axis in water and is gone by 5°, where the bare photodiode accepts ±55°. tables/original_rescue_top.md lists the best combinations: all of them are a green or cyan LED with a lens in front of the photodiode, and reach 46–49 dB depending on which capacitance is taken.

The first amplifier's feedback resistor

The first amplifier (the transimpedance amplifier, TIA) turns photocurrent into voltage; its feedback resistor is its gain. The batch swept it from 10 kΩ to 100 MΩ for ten photodiodes, with the feedback capacitor changed each time to keep a 16 kHz bandwidth up to 1 MΩ. Above that the capacitor cannot be made smaller and the bandwidth falls, to 2–3 kHz at 100 MΩ.

The receiver's own noise, as a current at the photodiode, pA/√Hz at 1 kHz, on the v2 front end, which has no servo (tables/tia_rx_noise.md, batch c_tia; the v3 front end reads 13–24 % higher up to 100 kΩ, 0.66 at 100 kΩ, and its servo adds noise from 3.3 MΩ up with the large photodiodes):

Photodiode (capacitance)10 kΩ22 kΩ100 kΩ1 MΩ10 MΩ100 MΩ
SFH 2401 (65 pF)4.282.050.580.140.0420.016
MTD5052W at 600 pF4.282.050.580.150.0700.058
S1337-1010BR (1,100 pF)4.282.050.590.170.110.10
S3204-08 (1,600 pF)4.292.060.600.200.150.15
PIN-25DP (60,000 pF)7.065.945.585.545.535.53
  • Up to about 100 kΩ the noise falls in direct proportion to the resistor, and it is the same for every photodiode. That is because the noise there is not the first amplifier's. It is the noise of the later stages (the volume control and the ×310 gain stage), which looks smaller at the photodiode the more gain the first amplifier has in front of it. v2's 2.05 pA/√Hz is this, and it is why v3's 100 kΩ resistor is worth 8 dB.
  • Between 100 kΩ and 1 MΩ it changes over, and from 1 MΩ up it falls as the square root, because the resistor's own thermal noise is what is left.
  • Then it stops, at a floor set by the photodiode's capacitance. The amplifier's input voltage noise drives a current through that capacitance: 0.10 pA/√Hz for the S1337's 1,100 pF and 5.5 pA/√Hz for the PIN-25DP's 60,000 pF, which is why that large detector disappoints at any resistor value. A 65 pF photodiode has not reached its floor even at 100 MΩ.

  • In the dark, a large photodiode wants about 470 kΩ to 1 MΩ. Beyond that nothing is gained.
  • In room light without a filter, 100 kΩ is already enough. From there the shot noise of the ambient light is the limit, and a larger resistor only brings the overload point closer. Without a servo (the v2 front end) the bare S1337 overloads above 100 kΩ in 0.5 W/m².
  • So the resistor, the filter and the hood are one decision. The less ambient light reaches the photodiode, the larger the resistor that is both usable and useful. v3's 100 kΩ with the filter, the hood and the servo sits where the amplifier is still the limit (42.3 dB against 48.2 dB for shot noise, section 1). A second batch swept the resistor with the filter and hood in place (next table).
  • With the filter and the hood, more than 100 kΩ still pays indoors, and the December build's amplifier does as well as v3's at the same resistor. S1337-1010BR at 15 ft under white-LED lamps (tables/rf_filtered.md, figure, batch c_rf_filtered):

The transient engine agrees with the closed form within 0.2 dB on five such cases, run at 15 and 30 ft with the volume turned down so the output does not clip (batch a_laptop4). Three things follow. On v3, going from 100 kΩ to 220 kΩ adds 2.5 dB indoors and 470 kΩ adds 3.6 dB (2.0 and 2.8 dB on v2 + hood); in bright light nothing is gained past 220 kΩ. The December build with a 100 kΩ resistor (and the matching capacitor) reaches 41.4 dB, 0.9 dB more than v3's 40.5 dB with the same resistor: at 15 ft indoors v3's 8 dB is the resistor, and v3's other changes are for what this table does not show (the servo for strong ambient light, the filtered supply rail). And without a servo the larger resistor overloads sooner: v2 + hood at 1 MΩ is already overloaded at 5 W/m² of lamp light, and in daylight it works up to 200 W/m² with 22 kΩ, 100 W/m² with 47 kΩ, 50 W/m² with 100 kΩ and 20 W/m² with 220 kΩ, where v3's servo keeps every one of those working to 200 W/m² or more (tables/rf_daylight.md, batch c_rf_daylight).

  • No resistor rescues the bare MTD5052W with a blue LED in room light, where it stops between −1 and +1 dB. In the dark it levels off near 3 to 4 dB if its capacitance is 600 pF; with the 5 pF of the older assumption it would pass 14 dB at 33 MΩ.
  • Not simulated: 150 of the 2,640 rows, all on the v3 front end at 3.3 MΩ and above. ngspice does not find the servo's operating point there. They are recorded as failed.

What the Oct 28 receiver needs, with its electronics unchanged

The rescue batch also kept Clayton's circuit exactly as drawn (MTD5052W and LMH34400) and changed only the optics and the LED. SNR by distance in indoor light (tables/original_lmh_options.md, batch c_original_rescue):

The transient engine agrees on the cases it ran (17.6 dB and a STOI of 0.84 for that two-lens case, −0.5 dB for the condenser alone, 10.0 dB for green with the condenser, 41.8 dB for the condenser with the 6.7° lens at a lower gain setting).

The MTD5052W behind that condenser sees only about ±3° in water, and the model's LMH34400 noise ignores the photodiode's capacitance, so these numbers are optimistic if the capacitance is 600 pF. Measuring that capacitance and the receiver's noise floor would settle it (section 12).

5. Water

Thirty-seven water descriptions were used: pure water, pool and tank waters, the Jerlov ocean types I to 9C (from two sources: modelled and measured), Petzold's three stations and a chlorophyll model. The pool types rest on one published 451 nm measurement and assumptions; no absorption and scattering spectrum for chlorinated pool water was found. Petzold's stations were measured at one wavelength (514–530 nm) and are applied to every color, so they appear only in royal-blue results and never in a color comparison.

Which color carries furthest. Range to 14 dB in the dark, bare S1337 on the v3 amplifier, bare LED, with all scattered light counted as lost (tables/water_led_range_dark.md):

WaterViolet 405Royal blue 452Blue 465Cyan 500Green 522Red-orange 626
Pure fresh water717974554928
Tap-water tank667369524728
Clear pool495351413826
Pool, organics-shaped loss405354474428
Murky pool363837313023
Clear ocean, Jerlov IB (measured)323535313124
Ocean, Jerlov II (measured)262929262522
Coastal, Jerlov 1C (measured)161818171716

  • Royal blue is best or tied in every water a diver would train in. Blue 465 nm catches up only where dissolved organic matter eats the short wavelengths.
  • The color matters less as the water gets worse. In coastal water the colors shown land within 2 ft of each other, because scattering, which is nearly the same for every color, has taken over, and dissolved organic matter absorbs the blue. The textbook advice that green is the coastal color applies to links tens of metres long; over 15–50 ft the LED's efficiency outweighs it.
  • Red is never close. Water absorbs 0.3–0.4 /m at 630–660 nm, 30 to 45 times its absorption in the blue.
  • A white LED is a hedge in dirty water, where ambient light is weak. With the scattered light counted as below, an unfiltered cool-white LED matches or edges out royal blue in the coastal types (38 ft against 36 ft in Jerlov 1C, 34 against 30 in 3C; tables/water_led_range_mc.md), because its phosphor light is green-yellow, where that water is clearest. It cannot sit behind a narrow filter, so this holds only while ambient light is weak: in indoor light behind a hood it is still 2 ft ahead in those waters, and royal blue stays ahead in every pool water (tables/water_led_range_finished_v2_hood.md, figure for v3, batch c_led_water_finished: each color with its matched filter in the finished receivers).

Scattered light is not lost. The table above uses Beer–Lambert with the total attenuation c = a + b, which treats a photon as gone the moment it is scattered. Particles in water scatter mostly forward, within a few degrees, and a bare LED lights a wide cone. So for each photon scattered away from the straight line to the receiver, another is scattered onto it from the neighbouring direction. The Monte Carlo batch traced 4 million photons per case through 12 waters to estimate this.

On the LEDFraction of scattered light still collected (receiver accepting ±30° in water)
Nothing (135° beam)0.94
34° lens (Carclo 10196)0.82
14.5° lens (Carclo 10412)0.69
6.7° lens (Carclo 10003)0.55
5° lens (Carclo 10048)0.49

Median over all waters and distances; the spread across waters and distances is ±0.02 for the 34° lens and up to 0.16 for the narrow ones (tables/mc_scatter_recovery.md). A receiver that accepts only ±10°, like the hooded ones, collects about 0.82 from the bare LED. Two readings of this:

  • For the bare LED, the water's absorption sets the range, not its cloudiness. A pool at the 0.5 NTU legal turbidity limit (taken as 0.5 /m of scattering, an assumption) costs the December build 9 ft of range, from 36 ft to 27 ft, where Beer–Lambert says 21 ft, to 14.6 ft.
  • A narrow beam loses more to scattering than a wide one, because light scattered out of a narrow beam is not replaced. A lens still wins by a wide margin (next table), but by less in cloudy water than in clear.

6. Lenses

On the transmitter

P6's LED has no lens and spreads its light over a 135° cone. At 15 ft a 10 × 10 mm detector catches about two millionths of it. A small moulded lens over the LED narrows the cone and raises the intensity on the axis; the vendors publish that as candela per lumen. Eighteen lenses from Carclo and LEDiL were modelled.

Lens on the LEDBeam in airOn-axis gain, dB opticalSNR at 15 ft, dBSNR at 30 ft, dBLargest pointing error still above 14 dB at 30 ft
none135°040.926.930°
Carclo 1019634°+9.050.743.820°
Carclo 1019522°+12.051.347.920°
Carclo 1041214.5°+15.951.650.510°
Carclo 1019411°+18.051.651.110°
Carclo 100036.7°+21.351.651.57.5°
Carclo 100485°+23.951.651.65°

v3 receiver; pointing errors are in water, where every beam is about three-quarters as wide as in air (tables/tx_optics.md).

  • A lens is worth twice its optical gain while the amplifier is the limit. At 30 ft the 34° lens adds 9 dB of light and 17 dB of SNR.
  • Past the ceiling, a narrower lens buys range, not quality. At 15 ft every lens gives about 51.6 dB, the transmitter-noise ceiling. The narrower ones keep that out to longer distances and give it up in aiming tolerance.
  • The 34° lens is the practical one for hand-held divers. It holds above 40 dB out to 20° of pointing error at 15 ft and extends v3's range from 51 ft to 93 ft in a clear pool. The 5° lens needs the diver to hold aim within 5°.
  • Caution on the model. Each lens is a Gaussian beam of its published width and peak. Real lenses spill some light outside the main beam, so the fall-off at large angles is gentler than drawn; the on-axis values are the vendors' numbers.

On the receiver

SNR at 15 ft on the v3 amplifier with the FBH450-40 filter in indoor light, at 0°, 10° and 20° off the receiver's axis in water. A dash means no signal reaches the detector at that angle (tables/rx_optics_on_axis.md, batch c_rx_optics):

In front of the photodiodeS1337-1010BR (10 mm)SFH 2401 (2.85 mm)MTD5052W (1.2 mm)
nothing39 / 39 / 3622 / 22 / 19−15 / −15 / −20
hood, 1 in tube41 / 41 / 3023 / 22 / 7−15 / −15 / –
hood, 2 in tube41 / 34 / –23 / 11 / –−15 / – / –
ACL25416U-A condenser (23 mm, f = 16 mm)49 / 49 / –50 / – / –28 / – / –
ACL5040U condenser (45 mm, f = 40 mm)51 / – / –51 / – / –23 / – / –
FRP232 Fresnel (46 mm, f = 32 mm)51 / – / –51 / – / –27 / – / –
  • A lens trades field of view for area, and the trade is fixed by the detector's size. A lens can only concentrate light onto the detector from directions within about (detector half-width ÷ focal length) of its axis. For the 10 mm S1337 behind the 16 mm condenser that is ±10° in water. For the 2.85 mm SFH 2401 the response holds to about 4° and is gone by 8°; for the MTD5052W it falls from 2° and is gone by 5°.
  • So a lens turns a small photodiode into a large one with a narrow view. The SFH 2401 with the condenser matches the S1337 with it on axis (50 dB against 49 dB) with a detector one-twelfth the size, but must be pointed within about 4°.
  • A hood costs nothing on axis and removes ambient light. The 1 in hood keeps full signal out to about 10° in water and cuts ambient light to 19 %; the 2 in hood cuts it to 5 % and narrows the view to about ±5°.
  • Caution on the model. The lens entries assume a blur spot of one-sixteenth of the focal length; no ray trace was done, and the model lets the spot walk off the detector linearly, which is 12–25 % generous in field of view.

Flat ports or domes

A flat window makes the LED's beam narrower in water (refraction concentrates it by n² = 1.78) and makes the receiver's view narrower too. A dome keeps both wide.

Both ends off axis by0°10°20°30°40°50°
v3 without hood, flat ports39.038.736.220.8−29.8none
v3 without hood, dome ports29.329.127.923.811.8−12.8

Flat ports are 10 dB better when aligned, and domes are better beyond about 28° of error on both ends (batch c_dome). Half of the 10 dB is the LED's beam, which the flat port narrows. The other half is on the receiver: behind a dome the detector keeps its wide view in water, and by the same rule of optics it then looks smaller from the water by n². For a link that is aimed by hand within 20°, flat ports are the right choice.

7. Ambient light, filters and flicker

Steady ambient light

v3 at 15 ft under white-LED lamps with smooth 5 % flicker (batch c_ambient):

In front of the S1337Dark0.5 W/m² (indoor pool)5 W/m² (very bright hall)50 W/m² (daylight near the surface)
nothing42.031.922.7overload
hood only42.038.029.4overload
FBH450-40 only41.537.629.119.8

FBH450-40 + 2 in hood41.541.239.232.2
LEE 119 gel + FGB39 glass ($46) + 1 in hood34.133.429.921.2
  • In the dark a filter can only cost signal. The FBH450-40 costs 0.5 dB; the gel stack costs 8 dB because it passes only 37 % of the blue.
  • Filter and hood multiply. Each removes about 6–7 dB worth of ambient shot noise in bright light, and together 13 dB.
  • White-LED pool lamps are the worst case for a 450 nm filter. A white LED is a blue LED under a phosphor, and its blue peak sits at 445–455 nm, inside the filter's passband. Under white-LED lamps the filter passes 1.8 times the ambient current it passes under a flat spectrum of the same brightness, and 5 times what it passes under incandescent light (batch c_ambient, column ambient_dc_na; tables/ambient_spectra_filters.md has the SNR).
  • A short-pass filter is as good as the band-pass for blue. The Thorlabs FESH0500 (passes below 500 nm) gives 35.2 dB against the FBH450-40's 35.8 dB at 5 W/m², and also passes violet and 465 nm blue LEDs. This comparison is under white-LED lamps. The model stops at 780 nm, so how well the short-pass blocks the near infrared of incandescent light or daylight was not checked (see the near-infrared row in section 11). The daylight table further down used the FBH band-pass filters only, so it is not affected.

Filters and arrival angle

An interference filter (the FBH and Edmund band-passes, the FESH short-pass) passes a band that moves toward the blue as light arrives further off its axis. Behind a flat port the angle on the filter is also larger than the angle in the water. So the filter, not only the hood, limits the field of view.

Share of the royal-blue LED's light that each filter passes, by the receiver's pointing error in water (no hood; tables/filter_angle_transmission_XPE2RoyalBlue.md, batch c_filter_angle):

Filter0°10°20°25°30°40°
FBH450-40 (band-pass 430–470 nm)0.940.920.690.400.130
Edmund 84-782 (band-pass)0.910.910.820.620.300
FBH460-10 (10 nm wide)0.320.380.330.160.040
FBH470-40 (band-pass 450–490 nm)0.570.700.930.950.840.12
FESH0500 (short-pass, below 500 nm)0.990.990.990.990.970.44
LEE 119 gel + FGB39 glass (absorbing)0.370.370.370.370.370.37
  • The FBH450-40 is good to about ±15° and nearly gone by 30°. That is wider than the 1 in hood's ±10°, so in the proposed receivers the hood sets the field of view and the filter costs nothing more. Without a hood the filter would be the limit.
  • A short-pass filter has no such limit until 30°, because moving its edge toward the blue still leaves the LED inside the passband. With its on-axis result within 1 dB of the band-pass in bright light (Steady ambient light), it is the better choice for a receiver without a hood.
  • A filter centred a little red of the LED improves off axis. The FBH470-40 passes 57 % of the 452 nm LED on axis and 93–95 % at 20–25°, and under white-LED lamps it matches the FBH450-40 on axis (28.9 dB against 29.1 dB at 5 W/m²) and beats it at every angle beyond 5°. Read the on-axis tie with care: the model puts ambient light through each filter's straight-on curve, and by a later estimate that overstates the FBH450-40's ambient and understates the FBH470-40's when there is no hood (see the filter-angle row in section 11), so on axis the FBH450-40 is probably a few dB ahead.
  • Absorbing filters (gels, coloured glass) do not shift at all, but pass much less of the LED.

Lamp flicker

Smooth 120 Hz flicker does nothing to any v2 or v3 design at any depth tested, up to 20 %: the 5th-order 400 Hz high-pass removes it (−52 dB). Flicker shaped like rectified mains is different, because its harmonics at 240, 360, 480 Hz and up are inside the speech band.

v3 at 15 ft, FBH450-40 and 1 in hood, white-LED lamps, SNR in dB:

Under a flat-spectrum lamp the 5 % rectified case at 0.5 W/m² reads 16.2 dB (this is v3's "15.4 dB" case, corrected); under white-LED lamps it is 10.9 dB because of the blue peak described above. Batch c_flicker_fixes (grid).

The FBH460-10 row is probably too good. Lamp light enters the 1 in hood up to about 26° off axis, where the 10 nm passband has slid onto the lamps' 450 nm peak, and the model does not apply that shift to ambient light. A later estimate puts its ambient current up to 1.7 times higher than simulated behind the 1 in hood, which would leave about +2 dB of the +7 dB (1.3 dB less behind the 2 in hood). The FBH450-40 rows are not affected (section 11).

  • Detector size is irrelevant here. A detector 18 times smaller loses 0.8 dB. Hum and signal both scale with area.
  • A lens on the LED is the strongest fix, worth twice its optical gain, because it raises the signal without touching the ambient light.
  • A higher high-pass corner raises the SNR number but not intelligibility. Moving the corner from 400 to 600 Hz gains 4 dB against rectified flicker, but STOI does not rise (0.84 to 0.83 under a flat-spectrum lamp, 0.81 to 0.80 under white-LED lamps), because the same filter removes speech (figure, batches c_hpf and b_hpf).
  • The first bench task from v3 stands: look at the pool lights with a photodiode and a scope. If their flicker is smooth or absent, none of this matters.

The best-combination search of section 6 was repeated under hard conditions: a murky pool and 2 W/m² of white-LED light with 5 % rectified flicker. Hum is the lowest of the four limits in 88 % of its 20,160 rows (9,520 combinations of parts at 15 and 30 ft; cool white, which has no matched filter, is entered twice), and 39 % of the rows reach 14 dB without overloading the front end. Combinations that overload the front end are left out of each median; at 30 ft that is under 3 % of any option's combinations in the hard conditions and under 9 % in the clear pool.   • Bare or behind a hood, every photodiode of about 8 mm² or more gives the same result. Hum and signal both grow with detector area, so area cancels: −19 dB bare whatever the size. The two smallest fall behind once a hood has removed most of the hum, because the amplifier's own noise then shows.
  • A lens changes the ratio. The signal comes from one direction, so the lens gathers it over its whole aperture and puts it on the detector. Ambient light comes from every direction, and a detector behind a lens only receives the part arriving within its narrow field of view. The smaller the detector, the narrower that field: the signal stays, the ambient falls. A 1.2 mm² photodiode behind a 23 mm condenser is 51 dB better than the same photodiode bare, and 36 dB better than the 100 mm² S1337 behind its hood. This is the étendue rule of optics: light can be concentrated onto a smaller area only by accepting it from a narrower range of directions.
  • A hood does the same thing gently. It narrows the field of view without gathering more signal: 15 dB for the 1 in hood, 26 dB for the 2 in hood.

8. What the numbers mean for speech

SNR is a ratio of powers. STOI (short-time objective intelligibility) is a score from 0 to 1 that compares the receiver's output with the clean clip in frequency bands like those of the ear. Engine B makes a waveform for every run, so it gives both. In this model STOI runs from about 0.37 (noise only) to 0.92 (clean speech through the receiver's 300–3000 Hz band).

The 14 dB requirement corresponds to a STOI of 0.75. All 500 runs of the distance batch fall within about 1 dB of one curve, whatever the receiver, lens or water (tables/stoi_vs_snr.md):

STOI0.500.600.700.750.800.850.90
SNR needed, dB (v3)−4.72.59.413.518.324.135.0
  • Above about 25 dB, more SNR buys almost nothing a listener can use. v3's 40.9 dB and v2 + hood's 32.7 dB at 15 ft score 0.910 and 0.895. v3's advantage is range and margin, not quality at the demo distance.
  • Below 14 dB the score falls quickly: at 9 dB it is 0.70 and at 0 dB about 0.57, less than half way from noise only to clean.

Hum scores better than hiss at the same SNR. This is the one place where SNR and STOI disagree, and it matters for the flicker risk in section 7.

When rectified lamp flicker sets the SNR, the same SNR scores much higher: STOI reaches 0.75 at about 4 dB instead of 13.5 dB. Hiss covers every frequency band at once. Hum is a few steady tones (240, 360, 480 Hz and up), so it hides only the narrow bands it sits in and the ear, like STOI, reads the speech from the bands between them.

v3 at 15 ft under white-LED lamps, SNR in dB and STOI (tables/flicker_stoi_v3_15ft.md, batch b_flicker):

  • The high-pass change is confirmed as worthless: +4 dB of SNR, no change in STOI.
  • v2 + hood and v3 score the same under flicker (10.9 dB and 0.80–0.81 for both), because hum does not depend on the amplifier.
  • Caution. STOI was designed and tested for noise-like interference. A buzz that leaves the words readable can still be tiring to listen to, so this needs a listening check. Three of these runs kept their audio for that: 5 % flicker as proposed, the same with the 34° lens and 20 % flicker in bright light.

A second voice. The second test clip (a female synthetic voice) scores 0.8 dB lower in SNR and 0.02–0.05 lower in STOI at every distance on the v2 and v3 receivers (tables/voice2.md). The transient engine gives the same differences in 16 runs of its own (batches a_voice2 and a_voice3: 0.9 dB and 0.03–0.05 STOI). The conclusions do not depend on the clip, but both clips are synthetic speech; a recorded diver's voice through a mask has not been tried.

Every LED with every photodiode, as a score. The matrix of section 3 in STOI: figure, table. Any LED from violet to green scores 0.84 or better into a bare detector of 33 mm² or more at 15 ft.

9. Circuit settings

The transmitter

Four things on P6 change how much light carries the speech. All of them scale the signal, so each is worth the same number of dB at every distance until the 51.7 dB ceiling or the limiter is reached (tables/tx_drive_p1_sense.md, tables/tx_drive_spl_leds.md, batch c_tx_drive).

Change on P6SNR at 30 ft into v3, normal speechGainWhat it costs
as built (P1 29.7 kΩ, R41 2 Ω, one LED)26.9 dB
P1 at 60 kΩ (v3 proposal T3)32.3 dB+5.4 dBthe limiter clamps 0.7 % of the time for a loud talker (95 dB SPL)
P1 at 90 kΩ35.1 dB+8.2 dBclamps 1.6 % of the time for a loud talker, 4.8 % at 101 dB SPL
P1 at 120 kΩ36.8 dB+9.9 dBclamps 0.7 % of the time in normal speech, 6.8 % at 101 dB SPL
compressor (SSM2167, v3 proposal T2)35.8 dB+8.9 dBan added IC; background noise rises in pauses
R41 at 1.5 Ω (LED bias 250 mA)29.3 dB+2.4 dBbattery current ×1.33; LED peak 346 mA
R41 at 1 Ω (LED bias 375 mA)31.2 dB+4.3 dBbattery current ×2; LED peak 519 mA, 601 mA for a loud talker
two LEDs at the same current each32.8 dB+5.9 dBa second driver branch
four LEDs38.5 dB+11.6 dBfour branches
  • Speech level is the largest swing of all. From a quiet talker (77 dB SPL at the microphone) to a very loud one (101 dB) the SNR moves 22.5 dB: 14.9 to 37.4 dB at 30 ft. Where the microphone sits in the mask matters as much as any circuit change.
  • By SNR, turning up P1 is free gain, up to a point (the intelligibility score below is less generous). As built, normal speech peaks at 260 mA where the limiter allows 300 mA, and most of the speech is far below its peaks. 60 kΩ gives 5.4 dB while the limiter clamps less than 0.1 % of the time in normal speech.
  • More LED current pays less than its ratio. Doubling the current gives 4.3 dB, not 6 dB, because the LED makes less light per ampere as the current rises.
  • A second LED is worth a full 6 dB and does not run into that droop, but P6's driver has one branch.
  • None of these moves the 51.7 dB ceiling, which is the preamp's noise against the speech at its input. They move the link toward it.
  • Not in the link grids: R41 at 1.2, 0.82 and 0.68 Ω, and P1 at 45 kΩ. P6's power-up run does not converge in ngspice with those values, although it does at 1.0 Ω and at 60 kΩ. The three resistor values were left out of the batch, and the 540 grid rows with P1 at 45 kΩ are recorded as failed. The driver check below suggests the cause is numerical (section 12).

By the intelligibility score, the preamp trim has an optimum. SNR counts only noise. When the limiter clamps the peaks of loud speech it distorts the speech; SNR does not see that and STOI does. v3 receiver, compressor off (tables/tx_drive_stoi.md, figure, batch b_tx_drive):

29.7 kΩ (as built)0.8820.9100.9070.8680.7680.8680.8880.863
60 kΩ0.9010.9080.8720.8380.8220.8880.8670.837
90 kΩ0.9070.8940.8500.8190.8490.8840.8480.819
120 kΩ0.9100.8740.8390.8040.8650.8680.8380.802
  • More gain helps a quiet talker everywhere, and a normal talker only where the link is short of SNR. At 30 ft, 60 kΩ takes normal speech from 0.868 to 0.888, and more gain brings it back down. At 15 ft the trim as built is already best for normal speech.
  • For a loud talker any increase costs. Limiter clamping for under 1 % of the time (60 kΩ at 95 dB SPL) lowers the score from 0.907 to 0.872 at 15 ft.
  • The compressor shows the same pattern more strongly, for a different reason. At 30 ft it raises a quiet talker from 0.768 to 0.855 and lowers a loud one from 0.888 to 0.830. The limiter never clamps with the compressor on; the loss is the compressor's own gain changes.
  • Caution. STOI compares how the loudness of the output rises and falls with that of the clean clip, so it may mark clipping and compression down harder than a listener would. Two audio files were kept to judge by ear: very loud speech as built and with P1 at 120 kΩ. Until that is done, 60 kΩ is a sound compromise and 90 kΩ or more is not.

Does the LED's forward voltage matter to P6?

Every link simulation uses one transmitter result, made with P6's royal-blue LED, whatever the LED color. That rests on P6's driver regulating the LED current. The driver check tested it: P6 in ngspice with a diode model fitted to each LED's datasheet forward-voltage curve (2.08 V for red to 3.18 V for violet at 350 mA), each with R41 at 2, 1.5, 1.0 and 0.68 Ω (tables/tx_led_check.md, batch tx_led_check, 64 cases on the loudest 1.2 s of the clip).

  • The LED current is the same for every LED. In all 38 cases that converged it is 126–252 mA around 188 mA at 2 Ω, and the 5 V rail never falls below 4.96 V. The waveforms differ from the royal-blue run by 2.5–3.3 % of the speech swing (rms), and a second model of the same royal-blue LED differs by 3.1 %, so that is solver noise and not a color effect. It is 0.3 dB at most.
  • Scaling by the sense resistor is good to a few percent. The grids take the 2 Ω result and multiply it by 2 Ω / R41. Against the directly simulated current that is within 3.5 % at 1.5 Ω, 5.5 % at 1 Ω and 9.4 % at 0.68 Ω.
  • The convergence failures look numerical. 26 of the 64 cases did not converge, in no pattern: 2 Ω fails with five of the LED models, and 0.68 Ω, which fails with P6's own LED model, converges with eight others. A stability limit of the real current loop would not come and go with the LED's forward voltage. A bench check is still the way to be sure before R41 is changed.

The receiver's volume control

In the v2 and v3 receivers the volume control sits before a fixed gain stage (×310), so it turns down the speech but not that stage's hiss. At full volume the output stage clips whenever the link is strong. A listener has to turn the volume down at close range, and the SNR they get is the one at that setting, not the full-volume number in the grids.

Distancev2 + hood: highest volume without clipping, SNR therev3: highest volume without clipping, SNR therev3 at full volume (grid value)
1 ft−55 dB, 48.4 dB−55 dB, 47.8 dB51.6 (clips)
5 ft−30 dB, 45.3 dB−30 dB, 45.1 dB51.1 (clips)
10 ft−12 dB, 40.0 dB−12 dB, 45.6 dB47.0 (clips)
15 ft−6 dB, 32.7 dB−6 dB, 40.4 dB40.9 (clips)
20 ft and beyondfull, as the gridsfull, as the gridsdoes not clip

Volume steps of 0, −6, −12, −20, −30, −40 and −55 dB were tried (tables/volume_distance.md, batch c_volume_distance).

  • Inside about 10 ft the real ceiling is 40–50 dB, not 51.7 dB, because of the gain stage's hiss at reduced volume. That is still far more than a listener can use (section 8).
  • The volume must never be left low at long range. At 30 ft, v3 gives 26.9 dB at full volume, 19.8 dB at −20 dB and 0.9 dB at −40 dB. A receiver whose volume was set at 3 ft and then carried to 30 ft would fail. This is the argument for the automatic gain option of v3, or for moving the gain ahead of the volume control.
  • The transient engine cannot show output clipping. The TPA6211A1 vendor model stops when it is driven into clipping, so every transient run was made at a volume a listener would use, and the fast engines flag clipping instead (audit summary).

The automatic-gain option

v3's option for hands-free use puts an SSM2167 automatic gain stage in the receiver, with or without the same chip as a compressor in the transmitter. These receivers change their gain with the signal, so only the transient engine can run them. Clear pool, indoor light, normal speech (tables/agc_distance.md; every run is in tables/agc_runs.md):

DistancePlain v3 (volume set by hand): SNR dB, STOIAutomatic gain in the receiverCompressor in the transmitter and automatic gain
5 ft45.2, 0.9128.3, 0.7630.8, 0.76
10 ft44.7, 0.9130.1, 0.7634.8, 0.77
15 ft40.5, 0.9129.5, 0.7737.3, 0.78
20 ft35.0, 0.9027.7, 0.7836.7, 0.79
30 ft27.0, 0.8724.4, 0.7933.7, 0.81
40 ft20.3, 0.8221.6, 0.7230.8, 0.78
60 ft9.7, 0.7015.2, 0.5923.5, 0.64
80 ft1.2, 0.583.2, 0.5614.4, 0.63
  • It does what it is for. From 5 to 30 ft the speech level at the headphones only falls from 177 to 105 mV, 4.5 dB, where the plain receiver's level changes by more than 30 dB and has to be followed by hand. At 15 ft it stays between 134 and 142 mV in murky and cloudy water, in bright light and 10° off axis. That removes the volume problem described above.
  • By both measures it scores below the plain receiver out to about 60 ft. From 5 to 30 ft the automatic-gain receiver scores 0.76 to 0.79 where the plain v3 receiver scores 0.87 to 0.91. Only at 80 ft, where the plain receiver has run out of signal, does the full option score higher (0.63 against 0.58). Automatic gain turns itself up in the pauses between words, which brings the hiss up there, and it flattens the rise and fall of loudness that STOI compares.
  • Under rectified flicker it is worse off than the plain receiver: 6.5 dB and 0.72 against 16.1 dB and 0.84 for 5 % flicker at 0.5 W/m² under the same flat-spectrum lamp, because it turns the hum up in the pauses as well. With the compressor in the transmitter too it is 12.7 dB and 0.75.
  • Caution. Both measures count a gain change as damage, and a listener may not. This is the comparison where a listening test matters most.

10. Robustness

What is not known

The uncertainty batch drew 2,000 random combinations of the inputs nobody has measured yet and ran every preset against each. The ranges are assumptions: speech level 77–101 dB SPL, photodiode responsivity ×0.8–1.1, ambient light 0.1–5 W/m² from white-LED lamps, flicker of 5 or 20 % that is smooth in 60 % of draws (1,188) and rectified in 40 % (812), water from a tap-water tank to a cloudy pool, pointing error up to 10° at each end, LED junction 30–60 °C, LED wavelength ±5 nm, battery 3.3–4.1 V.

Share of draws at or above 14 dB (tables/uncertainty.md, batch c_uncertainty):

Receiver15 ft, smooth flicker15 ft, rectified flicker30 ft, smooth flicker30 ft, rectified flicker
Oct 28 receiver0 %0 %0 %0 %
v299.7 %1.5 %57 %0 %
v2 + hood100 %22 %62 %1.4 %
v3100 %22 %91 %1.4 %
v3 without hood100 %1.5 %78 %0 %
  • If the pool lights flicker smoothly or not at all, the December build passes at 15 ft in every one of the draws. Nothing else in the list can make it fail there.
  • If the flicker is rectified, the outcome depends on the lamps, not on the design. Of those draws, 22 % pass 14 dB with a hooded receiver, and 45 % reach 4.7 dB, the level at which hum-limited speech scores like hiss-limited speech at 14 dB (section 8).
  • What moves the result (rank correlation with SNR at 15 ft, v2 + hood; tables/uncertainty_drivers.md): rectified flicker −0.82, speech level +0.43, ambient light −0.16, flicker depth −0.11. Pointing within 10°, LED temperature, LED wavelength, battery voltage and photodiode responsivity are all under 0.05: they do not matter for v2 or v3.
  • For the Oct 28 receiver speech level (+0.87) and the LED's wavelength bin (+0.24) are what move it, and 95 % of the draws are more than 49 dB short at 15 ft.

The same draws with a lens on the LED

The 2,000 draws were run again with a lens on P6's LED (tables/uncertainty_lens.md, batch c_uncertainty_lens). Share of draws at or above 14 dB, December build (v2 + hood):

These are shares of assumed ranges, not probabilities. v3 gives the same percentages as the December build with each lens at 15 ft, because hum does not depend on the amplifier.
  • At 30 ft with smooth flicker the lens removes the remaining risk: 62 % becomes 99.9 %.
  • The draws include up to 10° of pointing error at each end, so the 14.5° lens's better numbers assume the diver holds that aim.

Repeatability

  • Noise seed. Eight repeats of the same run with different random noise differ by 0.03 dB in SNR (standard deviation) and 0.001–0.002 in STOI at 15 ft (tables/seed_spread.md). Differences smaller than 0.1 dB or 0.005 STOI in this report are not meaningful.
  • Test clip. See section 8: 0.8 dB and 0.02–0.05 STOI between two synthetic voices.

11. How far to trust the numbers

What was checked.

  • The code was audited before any run. Three independent audits and a code review found ten errors that changed results in v1–v3 or would have in v4, and all were fixed or documented first (audit summary). Nine more problems were found while the campaign ran; each is listed there with what was done.
  • The three engines agree. The fast engines rest on the same ngspice netlists as the full waveform simulation, and every transient run of a linear receiver was repeated through both of them with the same arguments. Over 304 such runs, engine B's SNR differs from the transient engine's by a median of −0.08 dB (90 % of runs within 0.12 dB, largest 0.27 dB) and engine C's by −0.10 dB (90 % within 0.15 dB, largest 0.24 dB). Engine B's STOI is within 0.02 of the transient engine's in all 305 runs (engine check). The automatic-gain receivers are not in this comparison; only the transient engine can run them.
  • The 1–2 dB that the older reports lost at high SNR was solver error. The transient engine's original SNR figure subtracts a noise-free run from a noisy one, and the two differ slightly while speech is playing. With ngspice's tolerance made ten times tighter, three check runs rise from 32.1, 38.9 and 42.7 dB to 32.7, 40.5 and 44.8 dB, within 0.1 dB of their values with the noise taken from the pauses (batch check_A_reltol). The fast engines never had this error.
  • The two machines agree. Five transient runs were made on both the laptop and the desktop; their results are identical to the last digit recorded.
  • The grids are repeatable. Five times during the night, rows drawn at random from the closed-form batches were computed again from nothing: each row's receiver was characterized again in ngspice into an empty folder. The passes took 688 rows from the 34 batches finished by 03:00, 871 rows from 43 batches at 04:45, 1,072 rows from 44 batches at 07:50, 1,183 rows from 45 batches at 07:57, and 1,195 rows from all 46 batches after the last one had run. Every compared value came out identical in all five (final pass, first, second, third, fourth). This matters because several batches ran side by side and shared one cache of circuit results.
  • 28 known-answer tests cover the metrics, the optical channel and the libraries (test_v4.py), and every library part was run through the channel model and sanity-checked (library check).

What the simulation cannot tell you. Agreement between engines shows the arithmetic is consistent. It does not show the model matches the hardware. In rough order of how much each could move a result:

Not known or not modelledWhich results it affectsLikely direction
Lamp flicker shape and depth at the pooleverything in the hum limitunknown; decides between "no effect" and "fails"
Absolute signal level: LED output, lens and port losses, photodiode response are datasheet typical values, several read from graphsevery hiss-limited SNR, 2 dB per dB of erroreither way; a ±1.5 dB optical error is ±3 dB of SNR
Pool water: no measured spectrum for chlorinated pool water was foundrange beyond about 20 fteither way
Scattered light: the large grids use Beer–Lambert; the Monte Carlo correction assumes particles that scatter like Petzold's measured ocean particlescloudy-water rangesthe grids are pessimistic; the correction could be off either way for pool particles

Lenses as ideal Gaussian beams; receiver lenses with an assumed blur spot, no ray traceoff-axis behavior of every lensfield of view 12–25 % generous

STOI under tonal humthe "hum is less harmful" findingneeds a listening check

FBH450-40 behind a hood, the proposed receivers' arrangement, is within 1 % (audit summary)

White-LED lamps and the FBH band-pass receivers are not affected (audit summary)
Output-stage clipping (the vendor model cannot run it)close range at high volumeflagged, not simulated

12. What to measure first

Each of these replaces an assumption that many results rest on. They are in order of how much they would settle.

  1. The pool lights. Photodiode and oscilloscope at the pool: is there flicker at 120 Hz, how deep, and is the waveform smooth or does it have sharp corners? Record the DC photocurrent of the S1337 behind its filter as well; that is the ambient level in the model's own units. This one measurement decides whether the flicker fixes are needed at all.
  2. The receiver's noise floor. Photodiode covered, output noise in the 300–3000 Hz band, divided by the gain. The model says 2.05 pA/√Hz at the input for v2 and 0.66 for v3. Every hiss-limited number scales with this.
  3. One absolute link measurement. The December build at one known distance in air or a tank: speech level and noise at the headphone output. The model says 32.7 dB at 15 ft in a clear pool. One point calibrates LED output, optics and response together; the distance law then gives the rest.
  4. A lens on P6's LED. A Carclo 10196 costs a few dollars. Expected: 9 dB more light on axis (17 to 18 dB of SNR while the amplifier or hum is the limit), still usable 20° off axis. It is the largest gain in the report and the strongest fix for hum.
  5. The MTD5052W's capacitance with an LCR meter at 0 V and under bias: 5 pF (the old assumption) or 500–700 pF (the 2021 datasheet).
  6. The LED's wavelength bin from the reel label or a spectrometer, if the MTD5052W stays in any test.
  7. Signal against distance in the actual pool, three or four distances. The slope beyond the inverse-square law is the water's attenuation.
  8. Listen to the hum examples in runs/b_flicker/ and judge whether a 10 dB SNR under hum is as usable as STOI says.
  9. Before changing R41 or P1 on P6, check the current loop on the bench: with P6's own LED model the simulator could not settle it at 1.2, 0.82 and 0.68 Ω (it could at 1.0 Ω) or at P1 = 45 kΩ. The driver check in section 9 suggests that is numerical, but only a measurement settles it.
